title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
formal: Do there exist constants \(K>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) and one deterministic multitape Turing machine that, on every positive integer \(n\) supplied in binary, outputs the exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell(n)\) in binary within \(K(b+1)^a\) steps, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\) is the input length?
definitions:
An addition chain for \(n\ge1\) is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
\[
1=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_r=n
\]
such that for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there exist indices \(j,k\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\}\) with \(a_i=a_j+a_k\). The two indices may coincide, and an earlier entry may be reused any number of times. The length is the number \(r\) of additions, not the number \(r+1\) of entries. Define \(\ell(n)\) as the minimum such length; in particular, \(\ell(1)=0\). The only initially available number is \(1\). Subtraction, division, multiplication of chain entries and additional initial constants are not chain operations. The sum need not use the immediately preceding entry.

The machine receives just the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with no leading zeros. Its output is the ordinary binary expansion of the integer \(\ell(n)\), with \(0\) written as a single zero bit. The same finite program and constants must work for all valid inputs. The program has the usual unrestricted finite alphabet and binary work tapes of a multitape Turing machine, but all work, input reads and output writing count in its worst-case step bound. It has no advice, oracle, random bits or uncharged preprocessing. Invalid input strings must be rejected within the same bound with \(b\) interpreted as their string length. No addition chain or auxiliary number-theoretic data are supplied.

The requested machine may use any deterministic computation to find the length; the restrictions on chain operations define the quantity being optimized, rather than restricting the machine's internal calculations. The output is only the optimal length, not a chain attaining it. The input is a single binary target, not a list of targets and not a unary string of length \(n\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and fixed polynomial bound satisfying the exact-output task for every \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. Exact integer output is part of this computational existence question, not an extra accuracy restriction on a numerical-value benchmark. A fast approximation, a heuristic, polynomial time in \(n\) instead of its bit length, or a result for special targets does not meet the stated guarantee. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption; hardness of forming several prescribed targets is a different problem.

context_blocks.text: Erickson’s exponentiation discussion distinguishes asymptotically short multiplication programs from computing the absolute minimum number of multiplications. The current book chapter still states the latter question. This card retains the earlier length-only target and does not infer an unproved equivalence with constructing an optimal chain.

The elementary bounds are \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\le\ell(n)\le2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor\), including \(n=1\). Thus an optimal chain has \(O(b)\) entries of at most \(b\) bits. The existence of short certificates does not supply a deterministic polynomial-time optimizer.

The cryptographic arithmetic paper distinguishes single-target optimality from multiple-target addition sequences. Its procedures for selected exponents are not a proof of the general exact polynomial-time claim.

The 2025 assembly-theory article describes the shortest-addition-chain complexity as unknown. Only that dated observation is used here; its broader claims about complexity classes and assembly models are not part of this card’s mathematical premises.

Wallner’s 2026 result concerns the expected decompressed size of restricted chain structures, including Brauer chains. An average over chains of a fixed length does not compute the unrestricted minimum length for a supplied target.

The separately catalogued Scholz–Brauer conjecture concerns a structural inequality for special exponents. That conclusion differs from a uniformly efficient computation of the optimum on every binary input.

why: Addition chains express reuse in multiplication-only exponentiation. Their optimal length is small enough to have short certificates, yet finding that length for an arbitrary binary exponent has resisted a general complexity classification.

importance.reason: A longstanding exact optimization problem at the intersection of arithmetic algorithms, circuit reuse and cryptographic exponentiation. Its single-target complexity is repeatedly distinguished from the solved hardness of the generalized problem; it is not a numerical special case of Scholz–Brauer.

sentences: An addition chain starts at one and repeatedly forms a new integer by adding two earlier entries.
Its shortest length is the fewest such additions needed to reach a specified positive target.
The target is given in binary, and the requested algorithm must output the exact optimum in time polynomial in that bit length.
This is a question about computing the minimum count, without additionally requiring an optimal chain as output.
Known short chains, restricted families, heuristics and hardness for multiple targets do not establish the requested general deterministic algorithm or its impossibility.
